blocks.x: Tom Cruise may be among the last of the old-school movie stars, but lately it seems like his career has been on autopilot. With action movie after action movie, especially those in the Mission Impossible franchise and Cruise’s unearthed IP like Top Gun and Days Of Thunder, it’s as if the man is turning in variations of the same performance we’ve seen before. It’s hard not to disappoint audiences that way and, as we saw with Mission: Impossible—The Final Reckoning, it is possible to underwhelm them with too much of the same. He is, at least, on a whole different frequency in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s lumbering Digger, often recalibrating the film’s orbit around his character and sometimes rescuing it from its own outsized ambitions.

“Digger” Rockwell (Cruise) is a wealthy Texas oil man whose business has gone global. He begins his day caring for his dying cat, a pathetic creature that has long outlived its shelf life because Digger is used to getting his way at any cost. His morning routine is interrupted by terrible news out of Greenland, where his equipment has caused a glacier shelf to break off and crash into continental Europe, causing widespread destruction and the deaths of hundreds of thousands. Summoned to a crowded war room including the President (John Goodman), a team of scientists lead by Ganesh (Riz Ahmed), and other high-ranking staff, Digger faces his toughest challenge yet: spinning the truth as global warming encroaches onto everyone’s doorsteps.

In opposition to the majority of Cruise’s play-it-safe role choices, Iñárritu has made a name for himself pursuing idiosyncratic works, to mixed results. No two of his movies look the same. From his international breakout with Amores Perros in 2000, Iñárritu announced himself as an auteur who pursued layered characters, often in parallel storylines. He returns to some of those interests again in Digger, following directly in the footsteps of his 2014 film, Birdman Or (The Unexpected Virtue Of Ignorance). Teaming up with yet another celebrated American movie star, he gives them one of their meatiest, least tethered roles in years. Both Michael Keaton and Cruise make the most of their movies’ zany premises, but in both cases, Iñárritu steals the spotlight. In trying to prove his cleverness with various cinematographic tricks, substance once again gets short shrift.

Digger‘s story is one of those “there’s more than meets the eye” situations, but once it’s all said and done, its environmental message lands with a “duh.” It’s retreading the global warming waters of Don’t Look Up with slightly varied villains (a pompous oil man instead of a goofy tech guru), but using the same blunt force to hammer home its message. We’re doomed if we let these bozos run our planet, yet here they are, taking up all the oxygen in the important rooms. But the thought isn’t much deeper than that sentiment. Although there are a lot of ideas in Digger, not all of them necessarily do more than point out the obvious or finish the thought; after it becomes this movie’s message that the rich have broken the earth, it’s a benevolent rich guy who uses his resources and technology to save the day. Maybe some rich people are okay, Digger says, but only if they learn from their relative’s shameful, destructive mistakes. There’s a slightly better critique of its president’s administration—no doubt drawing some parallels to our current one, in how it cashes in on religion for political points, making a big show of prayer circles but dispensing with them quickly when the faithful are no longer needed—but it’s only one of a handful of running bits in the movie that actually pay off.

So many people worked on the Digger script—including Iñárritu and his Birdman writers Nicolás Giacobone and Alexander Dinelaris, as well as Sabina Berman and an additional “story by” credit for Jez Butterworth—that there should be a clearer edge to the critique beyond “we’re cooked.” It seems as if Iñárritu was striving to create a modern version of Dr. Strangelove, but never finds the rhythm or wit. Instead, we get jokes like one of the characters suffering from cancer of the asshole. Digger becomes a cautionary tale about the destructive force of one’s man ego, which maybe Iñárritu could have paid better attention to.

It’s equally frustrating to see Iñárritu’s reunion with his longtime cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki come up with such garishly colorless images, as if someone spilled bleach on the wrong laundry cycle. In one scene, everyone around Digger is so washed out it looks like they’re covered in baby powder. Although there’s some fun theatrical staging in this scene, it might be easy to miss because just about everyone other than Digger is the same lifeless color. The lighting and color grading are so harsh, even co-stars like Goodman and Michael Stuhlbarg, playing the hapless Vice President, look like they’ve been prepped by the funeral home’s makeup artist.

Between the film’s structural and effects-driven tricks and twists, it certainly looks like Iñárritu wants to return to his Birdman roost. That roost will have to be shared with Cruise, who is what salvages Digger from fully becoming a stylish mess. The movie is very much Cruise’s show from the start, and whenever he’s on screen, even in crowded shots, he’s making expressions and having reactions we haven’t seen from him in decades. He brings back the hair-trigger temper and ego-driven bluster of the executive he played in Tropic Thunder, perhaps the last time he really swung for the fences. His makeup and hair also make use of the film’s noticeable desaturation, making him look older and more haggard than ever. His goal is to poke fun at American exceptionalism that gives way to ignorance, and Cruise relishes the chance to behave badly. It’s far more entertaining to watch Cruise chew through the scenery like overcooked steak than it is to wait for Iñárritu to finally find meaning in his movie.

The only issue with Cruise claiming the marquee spot is that no one else has much time to shine. While Goodman is enjoyably shifty and Ahmed has an incredible drunken scene, their time onscreen is relatively brief and deferential to Cruise. For co-stars like Sandra Hüller, Jesse Plemons, and Emma D’Arcy, there’s too little of them to leave a real impression of their characters, making way for Cruise to continue flexing his near-dormant acting muscles.

Yet, all this spectacle is for nothing. Digger lacks emotional depth, being much more interested in the showmanship of tricks and razzle-dazzle than character development. While Cruise puts on a good show, he’s walking around the loose threads of the script to get there. Digger may not be the return to Revenant form for Iñárritu after the debacle of Bardo, but Cruise steps in to sell the idea of a George W. Bush-like figure who’s selfish, full of bullshit self-made mythology, and will promise the world to whoever’s listening—as long as they agree with him. Perhaps only Cruise could find something worth digging into in the rubble of Iñárritu’s Ozymandias-sized epic.
Writers: Alejandro González Iñárritu, Sabina Berman, Nicolás Giacobone, Alexander Dinelaris
Cast: Tom Cruise, John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons, Emma D’Arcy
